summary: Points out gaps in the official Host-Host protocol found while building the network software. Cases such as error control messages, unusual message types, and messages flagged as coming from the IMP were not clearly described. The note suggests how implementations should handle these edge cases.

eli5.summary: A game's rulebook did not say what to do when something unexpected happens. A player writes down which odd situations came up and how to handle them.

subtitle: Clarifying edge cases found while implementing the Host-Host protocol

tldr.problem: While building NCP software, implementers found three areas where the official Host-Host protocol was unclear: error control messages, unusual message types from the IMP, and messages flagged as coming from the IMP.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC documents specific error conditions and proposes standardized ways to handle them, including clearer error codes and a RESET mechanism to sync state after host failures.
tldr.outcome: This provides implementers with a practical guide for handling exceptional cases and helps prevent protocol deadlock when systems fail.

today: RFC 117 provides practical guidance for early NCP implementations. These clarifications became part of the collective understanding as the network protocol matured.

sections.title: Gaps in the Protocol
sections.content:
RFC 117 identifies three areas where the official NCP protocol was incompletely specified: how to handle ERR error commands, how to handle unusual message types from the IMP (Interface Message Processor), and how to handle messages with the From-IMP bit set.

These situations arose frequently during experimental NCP implementation, even though they would never occur if every system operated correctly. The RFC notes that these error cases are excellent debugging tools for the protocol.
sections.eli5: When the early network was being built, implementers found strange cases the rulebook didn't explain. They document these cases and how to handle them properly.

sections.title: Error Command Specification
sections.content:
The RFC proposes a structure for ERR commands with a standardized 8-bit error code field, an 80-bit field to store the offending command, and additional fields for socket numbers and context information. This gives the remote system enough information to understand what went wrong.

For example, if a command is sent on a non-existent link, the error response should include the link number and part of the offending message. If allocation is exceeded, it should report how many bits and messages were sent versus allocated.
sections.eli5: Instead of sending vague error messages, the RFC suggests making them detailed: include what command failed, what sockets were involved, and what the system was trying to do at the time.

sections.title: Handling Host Failures
sections.content:
When a remote host or IMP goes down and then comes back up, the local NCP's table entries for connections to that host still exist, causing confusion. The RFC proposes a RESET mechanism: when an NCP starts up, it sends RESET commands to every other site. Each site responds with RESET-reply and sets an 'up-bit'. If a Type 7 or Type 9 error message indicates a remote host is down, the up-bit is cleared.

This ensures that when systems recover from failure, their connection tables are properly synchronized rather than holding stale entries.
sections.eli5: When a remote computer comes back online, it needs to tell everyone else 'start fresh with me'. The RFC suggests using RESET messages so old broken connections get cleaned up.
